title: What are the three ways to set a price, and when do you use each?
description: Pricing methods for case interviews. Ways to set a price once you know the floor and the ceiling. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: There are three common ways to set a price, and each one answers a different question. Knowing all three helps you sound balanced in a pricing case. Here they are.
body:
When it helps

Ways to set a price once you know the floor and the ceiling.

The checklist

Cost-plus

  • Unit cost × (1 + target markup)

Competitor-based

  • Match, undercut or charge a premium

Value-based

  • Share of the value the customer gets

Launch strategy

  • Skim: start high
  • Penetrate: start low

An example

A start-up makes software that saves accountants five hours a month. Cost-plus says: our cost is £8 a user, add 50%, charge £12. Competitor-based says: rivals charge £20 to £30. Value-based says: five hours of an accountant's time is worth around £150, so even £40 is a bargain. The three methods give very different numbers, which is exactly why a good answer looks at all three.

How it sounds in an interview

I'd look at the price from three sides: what it costs us, what rivals charge, and what it is worth to the customer. The answer usually sits between the cost floor and the value ceiling.

Compare the three price anchors

A manufacturer sells a replacement filter. Each unit costs £12 to produce and deliver. A competing filter sells for £20. Customers estimate that the manufacturer's better design saves them £6 of maintenance expense per filter. These numbers provide three anchors, not one automatic answer.

Cost-plus pricing might start at £12 plus a target margin. Competitor-based pricing suggests looking near £20, after adjusting for differences in quality and switching costs. Value-based pricing asks how much of the £6 extra customer benefit the company can capture. A £24 price may be plausible for some customers, but only if they believe and can realise the savings.

Test demand before concluding. At £20, selling 100,000 units generates £800,000 of contribution. At £24, contribution rises to £12 a unit; however, if sales fall to 60,000, total contribution is only £720,000. The higher unit margin produced a worse total result. Profit, not just price, is the objective.
